b: Solomon's temple, the kings of Judah, and the repeated cycle of reform and relapse. It ends with Cyrus's decree permitting the exiles to return, which is where Ezra picks up.

7.t: The people fall face down on the pavement. Chronicles adds this detail that Kings does not have.

Written to Israel under a specific covenant, and frequently applied to modern nations in ways the text does not support. The principle of humility and repentance stands; the national promise was theirs. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

36.h: He sent word again and again
36.t: Because he had pity on his people — until there was no remedy. The verdict on the whole history.
The Hebrew Bible ends here, with permission to go home. That is a deliberate place to stop.

16.h: The eyes of the LORD range
16.t: Looking for those whose hearts are fully committed. Said as a rebuke to a king who trusted an alliance instead.

20.h: We do not know what to do
20.t: Jehoshaphat's prayer facing invasion, ending with that admission and with eyes on God. The battle is won by singers going out in front.

34.t: He began seeking God at sixteen and purging idolatry at twenty. Chronicles gives his age deliberately.

1.t: Solomon asks for wisdom to govern, and is given wealth as well. Chronicles frames it as a test he passed.

5.t: The priests could not perform their service. The singers were in unison praising God when it happened.

6.t: Longer here than in Kings, and it anticipates exile and asks that prayers turned toward this place be heard.

14.t: Asa's prayer before battle: it is nothing for you to help the powerless against the mighty.

15.h: Be strong and do not give up
15.t: Azariah's word to Asa. The reform that follows is genuine and, as chapter 16 shows, not permanent.

17.t: Jehoshaphat sends officials and Levites out with the Book of the Law. A deliberate programme of teaching rather than a one-off reform.

26.t: Uzziah's pride led to his downfall. He burns incense in the temple and is struck with leprosy. Chronicles is repeatedly interested in what success does to kings.

30.t: Held late and by people who were not properly purified. Hezekiah prays that God would pardon everyone who sets their heart on seeking him, and God heard.

33.t: The worst king in Judah's history, taken to Babylon with a hook in his nose, humbles himself and is restored. Chronicles alone records it.

2.h: Who can build a house for him
2.t: Solomon asks it before he starts building. Humility at the beginning of the project.

3.t: Where Abraham offered Isaac, and where David saw the angel. Chronicles connects them deliberately.

4.t: Bronze sea and lampstands. Everything costly, all of it eventually carried to Babylon.

8.t: Building, trade and administration at the height of the kingdom.

9.t: Chronicles keeps the visit and omits Solomon's decline entirely.

10.t: Rehoboam's harshness divides the kingdom. The writer says the turn of events was from God.

11.t: Faithful Levites leave their land in the north to worship in Jerusalem. Faith costing property.

12.t: When Rehoboam abandons God, Egypt invades; when he humbles himself, destruction is withheld.

13.t: A king arguing theology to an enemy army before battle.

18.t: Told as in Kings, with Jehoshaphat's alliance with Ahab condemned in chapter 19.

19.t: Consider carefully what you do, for there is no injustice with the LORD. Justice treated as an act of worship.

21.t: He murders his brothers and dies to no one's regret. Chronicles records it bluntly.

22.t: The same crisis as 2 Kings 11 — the line of David down to one hidden child.

23.t: Jehoiada the priest restores the rightful king.

24.t: Joash kills the son of the priest who saved him. Jesus refers to this murder in Matthew 23.

25.t: He does right, but not wholeheartedly. Chronicles' verdict on a divided heart.

27.t: Because he walked steadfastly before the LORD.

28.t: He shuts the temple doors. Israel's northern soldiers return captives from Judah after a prophet rebukes them — mercy from an unexpected side.

29.t: In the first month of his first year. Reform was his first act, not an afterthought.

31.t: And he prospered. Chronicles' summary of a faithful king.

32.t: After his healing, his heart was proud. Even the best kings failed afterwards.

35.t: None like it since Samuel. And then, in chapter 35:20–27, he dies in a battle he was warned not to fight.
